docs.title: Digital Marketing & SEO Mastery Path
docs.text:
Mastery Path BOOTCAMP VINOD BHANUJA

A structured, module-wise digital marketing program that takes you from how the marketing funnel works to running real campaigns and planning a full year of growth — with step-by-step instructions, cheat sheets, and a hands-on exercise in every module.

You don't need to code. You need a browser, curiosity, and a real or practice business to market — every lesson is written so you can apply it the same day, whether you're a student, a small-business owner, a freelancer or a marketer moving up.

docs.title: 01 · Digital Marketing Fundamentals & the Funnel
docs.text: Digital marketing is the work of getting the right people to notice a business online, trust it, and take an action — buy, call, sign up or visit. This module gives you the map every later lesson hangs on: the funnel, the channels that feed it, and the numbers that tell you whether it works. We'll use one running example through Level 1: Chai Corner, a small café in Pune that wants more weekday customers and catering orders.

docs.title: 1. The marketing funnel
docs.text:
1. Awareness — people discover you exist: a Google search result, an Instagram Reel, a friend's WhatsApp forward.
  2. Consideration — they compare: read reviews, check your menu, look at prices and photos.
  3. Conversion — they act: order online, call, walk in, fill a catering enquiry form.
  4. Retention & advocacy — they come back and recommend you: loyalty offers, email or WhatsApp updates, review requests.
  5. Each stage loses people. If 10,000 people see Chai Corner's posts, 400 visit the website (4%), and 20 send an enquiry (5% of visitors), the funnel converts 0.2% overall. Improving any one stage lifts the final number.

docs.title: 2. The main channels
docs.text:
1. Search (SEO) — free, slow-building traffic from Google when people search things like "café near FC Road".
  2. Paid search (Google Ads) — pay per click to appear for those searches immediately.
  3. Social media (organic and paid) — Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, LinkedIn; great for awareness and community.
  4. Email and WhatsApp — direct, cheap retention channels you own.
  5. Content — blogs, videos and guides that answer questions and earn trust (and feed SEO and social).
  6. Referral and partnerships — influencers, affiliates, local collaborations.
  7. Owned (website, email list), earned (reviews, press, shares) and paid (ads) media work together — paid ads can kick-start awareness while owned channels build long-term value.

docs.title: 3. The numbers that matter
docs.text:
1. Impressions / reach — how many times / people saw something.
  2. CTR (click-through rate) = clicks ÷ impressions. 150 clicks from 5,000 impressions = 3%.
  3. Conversion rate = conversions ÷ visitors. 12 enquiries from 300 visitors = 4%.
  4. CPC, CPL, CPA — cost per click, per lead, per acquisition. ₹3,000 spend ÷ 12 leads = ₹250 CPL.
  5. ROAS = revenue ÷ ad spend. ₹18,000 revenue from ₹3,000 spend = 6× ROAS.
  6. CLV (customer lifetime value) — what a customer is worth over time. A regular who spends ₹200 twice a week for a year is worth far more than one visit, which justifies a higher acquisition cost.

docs.title: 4. Setting a SMART goal
docs.text:
1. Specific — "increase weekday catering enquiries", not "grow the brand".
  2. Measurable — a number you can track: 30 enquiries a month.
  3. Achievable — based on current numbers (10 a month today).
  4. Relevant — tied to revenue: catering orders average ₹6,000.
  5. Time-bound — within 90 days.
  6. Write it in one line: "Grow catering enquiries from 10 to 30 per month by 31 March, at a cost per lead under ₹300."

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Term Meaning Example Funnel Awareness → Consideration → Conversion → Retention 10,000 → 400 → 20 CTR Clicks ÷ impressions 150 / 5,000 = 3% Conversion rate Conversions ÷ visitors 12 / 300 = 4% CPL Spend ÷ leads ₹3,000 / 12 = ₹250 ROAS Revenue ÷ ad spend ₹18,000 / ₹3,000 = 6× CLV Value of a customer over time Regular customer vs one-time visitor Owned / earned / paid Website & list / reviews & shares / ads

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Every digital channel is a matching system: platforms like Google and Meta are trying to show each person the content most likely to keep them satisfied, and they charge advertisers or reward publishers accordingly. That's why relevance beats volume — a page or ad that closely matches what someone wants earns higher click-through rates, which platforms reward with better rankings or cheaper clicks. The funnel is simply a way to see where that matching breaks: low CTR means your message doesn't fit the audience, a low conversion rate means the page doesn't deliver what the click promised, and weak retention means the product or follow-up isn't earning a second visit. Marketing improves results by fixing the narrowest stage first.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Pick a real business (your own, a family business, or a local shop). Write: (1) one SMART goal, (2) the funnel stages with a realistic estimate of how many people reach each stage per month, and (3) the two channels you'd start with and why. Calculate the conversion rate from first stage to final action.

docs.title: 02 · Audiences, Personas & Customer Journeys
docs.text: Marketing to "everyone" reaches no one. This module shows you how to define exactly who you're talking to, what they care about, and the steps they take before buying — so every message, keyword and ad you create later has a target.

docs.title: 1. Segment the market
docs.text:
1. List the groups who could buy from the business. For Chai Corner: nearby office workers, college students, families on weekends, companies ordering catering.
  2. Describe each group by demographics (age, income, location), behaviour (when and how they buy) and needs (speed, price, quality, convenience).
  3. Score each segment on size, value per customer and how easily you can reach it. Office catering is small in number but high value (₹6,000 per order) and reachable through LinkedIn and Google searches.
  4. Choose one primary segment to focus on first, and one secondary.

docs.title: 2. Build a persona
docs.text:
1. Give the persona a name and role: "Neha, 31, admin manager at a 60-person IT firm in Baner."
  2. Goals: arrange reliable snacks for Friday team meetings without hassle.
  3. Pain points: late deliveries, vendors who don't send GST invoices, food that arrives cold.
  4. Where she looks: Google ("office snacks catering Baner"), colleague recommendations, Swiggy/Zomato reviews.
  5. Objections: "Can they handle 60 people? Will they invoice the company properly?"
  6. What convinces her: photos of past office orders, a clear per-head price, a GST invoice, and a quick WhatsApp response.
  7. Base personas on evidence — talk to 5 real customers, read reviews, check what people search — not guesses.

docs.title: 3. Map the customer journey
docs.text:
1. Trigger — Neha's manager asks for Friday snacks.
  2. Search — she Googles, sees three cafés and a catering aggregator.
  3. Evaluate — she opens two websites, checks the menu PDF and reviews.
  4. Contact — she sends a WhatsApp message to the one that shows a clear "Office catering" button.
  5. Purchase — confirms 60 portions, pays by UPI, receives a GST invoice.
  6. Experience — food arrives on time; the team likes it.
  7. Repeat — the café sends a monthly menu on WhatsApp; she reorders.
  8. For each step, note the touchpoint (Google, website, WhatsApp) and what could make her drop out. Those drop-off points become your marketing to-do list.

docs.title: 4. Write the value proposition
docs.text:
1. Use the format: For [persona] who [need], [business] is the [category] that [key benefit], unlike [alternative].
  2. Example: "For office admins who need reliable team snacks, Chai Corner is the local café caterer that delivers hot, GST-invoiced orders for 20–100 people on time — unlike aggregators that can't guarantee timing."
  3. Turn it into a headline (8–12 words) and three supporting points you'll reuse on the website, ads and social posts.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Tool Purpose Output Segmentation Find groups worth targeting 3–5 segments scored Persona One realistic buyer Goals, pains, channels, objections Journey map Steps before and after purchase Touchpoints + drop-off risks Value proposition Why choose you One sentence + headline Evidence sources Make personas real Interviews, reviews, search data

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Ad platforms and search engines reward relevance, and relevance is defined by the audience, not the business. A persona forces every later decision — keywords, ad copy, landing page layout, posting times — to be judged against one specific person's goals and objections. The journey map exposes that most lost sales happen in the middle: people who were interested but hit friction (no price, no reply, no trust signal). Fixing those moments is usually cheaper than buying more traffic.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: For your business from Module 1, create one primary persona (with goals, pains, channels, objections), a seven-step journey map with touchpoints and drop-off risks, and a one-sentence value proposition plus a headline. If you can, talk to two real customers and update the persona with what they say.

docs.title: 03 · Websites & Landing Pages That Convert
docs.text: All your marketing traffic lands somewhere. If that page is slow, unclear or hard to act on, every rupee spent on ads and every hour spent on SEO is wasted. This module teaches you to judge and improve a website and build a focused landing page.

docs.title: 1. What a website must do in five seconds
docs.text:
1. Say what you offer and for whom — a clear headline from your value proposition.
  2. Show proof — reviews, ratings, client logos, photos of real work.
  3. Make the next step obvious — one primary call-to-action (CTA): "Get a catering quote", "Order now", "Book a call".
  4. Load fast — test at pagespeed.web.dev; aim for the page to be usable within about 2–3 seconds on mobile.
  5. Work perfectly on mobile — in India most visits are on phones. Check text size, tap targets and that the CTA is visible without scrolling.

docs.title: 2. Anatomy of a landing page
docs.text:
1. A landing page has one goal and usually no main navigation menu, so visitors aren't distracted.
  2. Headline that matches the ad or search that brought the visitor ("Office snacks catering in Baner — hot, on time, GST invoice").
  3. Sub-headline with the key benefit and a number: "Trusted by 40+ Pune offices · 20–100 people".
  4. Hero image of the real product or service.
  5. Benefits in 3–4 short points (not features alone: "arrives hot" beats "insulated boxes").
  6. Social proof — two or three short testimonials with names and companies, star rating.
  7. Offer and price — "From ₹120 per person", or a clear starting price.
  8. Objection handling / FAQ — minimum order, delivery area, payment, invoices.
  9. CTA repeated at the top and bottom — form, WhatsApp button or phone tap-to-call.

docs.title: 3. Forms and CTAs
docs.text:
1. Ask only what you need: name, phone, date, number of people. Every extra field lowers completions.
  2. Write CTAs as outcomes: "Get my quote" beats "Submit".
  3. Add a WhatsApp click-to-chat link (https://wa.me/91XXXXXXXXXX?text=Hi%20I%20need%20catering) — many Indian customers prefer chatting to forms.
  4. Show what happens next: "We reply within 30 minutes, 9am–9pm."
  5. After submission, send people to a thank-you page — useful for confirming the lead and for conversion tracking later.

docs.title: 4. Tools to build pages without code
docs.text:
1. WordPress with a page builder (Elementor, Gutenberg blocks), Wix, Shopify (for stores) or Google Sites for a quick free page.
  2. Use a template, then replace every section with your persona-driven content.
  3. Compress images (TinyPNG or built-in optimisation) — large images are the most common cause of slow pages.
  4. Install analytics before launch (covered in Module 9) so you can measure from day one.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Element Good practice Headline Matches the ad/search; says what + for whom Proof Ratings, testimonials with names, real photos CTA One goal, outcome wording, repeated top and bottom Form 3–4 fields; WhatsApp alternative Speed Test at pagespeed.web.dev; compress images Mobile CTA visible without scrolling; readable text Thank-you page Confirms action; enables tracking

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A visitor's decision to stay or leave happens in seconds, driven by message match (does this page continue the promise I clicked on?) and cognitive load (how hard is it to understand and act?). Ad platforms also score your landing page: Google Ads' Quality Score includes landing page experience, so a relevant, fast page directly lowers your cost per click. Removing navigation, cutting form fields and adding proof all work the same way — they reduce the effort and uncertainty standing between interest and action.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Audit a real website using the five-second checklist and PageSpeed Insights (record the mobile score). Then write the full content for a one-goal landing page for your persona: headline, sub-headline, four benefits, two testimonials (real ones if you have them), price/offer, four FAQs and the CTA. Build it in Google Sites, Wix or WordPress if you can.

docs.title: 04 · How Search Engines Work (SEO Basics)
docs.text: SEO (search engine optimisation) is making your pages easy for search engines to find, understand and trust, so they appear when people search. This module explains how Google decides what to show, and sets up the free tool every SEO uses: Google Search Console.

docs.title: 1. Crawl, index, rank
docs.text:
1. Crawling — Googlebot follows links and sitemaps to discover pages.
  2. Indexing — Google reads each page (text, headings, images, structured data) and stores it in its index. A page that isn't indexed can never rank.
  3. Ranking — for each search, Google orders indexed pages by hundreds of signals: relevance to the query, quality and helpfulness of the content, links from other sites, page experience (speed, mobile, HTTPS), freshness and location.
  4. Serving — results appear as blue links, plus features like the map pack, images, videos, "People also ask" and AI-generated overviews.

docs.title: 2. The three pillars of SEO
docs.text:
1. Technical SEO — can Google crawl and index the site? Fast, mobile-friendly, secure (HTTPS), no broken pages (Level 2, Module 1).
  2. On-page SEO / content — does each page clearly answer a search? Titles, headings, useful content (Module 6).
  3. Off-page / authority — do other trustworthy sites link to and mention you? Reviews and citations matter for local businesses (Level 3, Module 1).

docs.title: 3. Search intent
docs.text:
1. Informational — "how to make masala chai". Wants an answer or guide.
  2. Navigational — "Chai Corner Baner". Wants a specific site.
  3. Commercial — "best catering for office in Pune". Comparing options.
  4. Transactional / local — "order samosa near me". Ready to act.
  5. Look at the current top results for a search: if they're all guides, a sales page won't rank; if they're all local listings, you need a Google Business Profile. Match the intent of what already ranks.

docs.title: 4. Set up Google Search Console
docs.text:
1. Go to search.google.com/search-console and add a property. Choose Domain (covers all versions of your site) and verify with a DNS TXT record at your domain provider, or choose URL prefix and verify with an HTML tag.
  2. Submit your XML sitemap under Indexing → Sitemaps (most CMSs create one at /sitemap.xml).
  3. Use URL inspection to check if a page is indexed and to request indexing for new pages.
  4. After a few days, open Performance: queries people used, impressions, clicks, CTR and average position.
  5. Check Pages (indexing report) for pages Google couldn't index and why.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Concept What to check Crawled? Sitemap submitted, pages linked internally Indexed? URL inspection → "URL is on Google" Relevant? Page matches the search intent Trusted? Links, reviews, brand mentions Performance Search Console → Performance (queries, CTR, position) Problems Search Console → Pages / Experience reports

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Google's index is an enormous inverted index — for each word and concept, a list of documents that contain it — which lets it find candidate pages for any query in milliseconds. Ranking systems then score those candidates: language models judge how well a page satisfies the meaning behind the query (not just matching words), link analysis estimates authority, and quality systems demote thin, copied or unhelpful pages. Because searchers' clicks and satisfaction feed back into how results are evaluated, the long-term SEO strategy is simple to state and hard to fake: be the most genuinely useful result for the people searching.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Set up Google Search Console for a site you control (a free WordPress or Blogger site is fine), submit the sitemap and inspect your home page. For five searches related to your business, note the intent type and what kind of pages rank in the top five. Write one sentence per search on what page you'd need to compete.

docs.title: 05 · Keyword Research
docs.text: Keywords are the words people type into search engines. Keyword research tells you what your audience is actually searching for, how often, and how hard it is to rank — so you create pages and ads for real demand instead of guessing.

docs.title: 1. Brainstorm seed keywords
docs.text:
1. Start from your persona's problems and the products you sell: "office catering", "snacks for meetings", "café Baner", "chai delivery".
  2. Add modifiers people use: location ("in Pune", "near me"), price ("cheap", "per plate"), quality ("best"), format ("for 50 people").
  3. Use Google itself: type a seed and note autocomplete suggestions, People also ask questions and related searches at the bottom.

docs.title: 2. Get volumes and ideas
docs.text:
1. Google Keyword Planner (free inside a Google Ads account: Tools → Keyword Planner → Discover new keywords). Enter seeds and location (e.g. Pune); it shows average monthly searches as ranges and top-of-page bid estimates.
  2. Google Search Console → Performance shows queries you already appear for — gold for existing sites.
  3. Google Trends compares interest over time and seasonality (e.g. "diwali gift hampers" peaks in October).
  4. Paid tools such as Ahrefs, Semrush or Ubersuggest add difficulty scores and competitor keywords; free tiers are fine for practice.

docs.title: 3. Judge each keyword
docs.text:
1. Volume — how many monthly searches. Local keywords are small (50–500) but valuable.
  2. Intent — informational, commercial, transactional or local (Module 4).
  3. Difficulty — how strong the pages already ranking are. Search the keyword: if the top results are big brands and directories with strong sites, it's hard for a new site.
  4. Business value — would this searcher buy? "office catering Baner" (20 searches, ready to buy) beats "chai recipe" (50,000 searches, won't buy catering).
  5. Favour long-tail keywords (3+ words, specific) when starting out — lower competition, clearer intent.

docs.title: 4. Organise into a keyword map
docs.text:
1. Group keywords with the same intent into a cluster: "office catering Pune", "corporate snacks Pune", "team lunch catering Pune" → one page.
  2. Assign one primary keyword per page and 3–6 secondary ones. Don't make two pages compete for the same keyword.
  3. Build a simple sheet:
Page Primary keyword Secondary keywords Intent Monthly volume /office-catering office catering pune corporate snacks pune, team lunch catering Transactional 210 /menu café menu baner chai and snacks baner, café prices Local 90 /blog/office-party-snacks office party snack ideas snacks for team meeting Informational 480

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Source Use Autocomplete / People also ask Real phrasing and questions Keyword Planner Volume ranges, bid estimates Search Console Queries you already rank for Google Trends Seasonality Long-tail Specific, easier, higher intent Keyword map One primary keyword per page

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Search volume numbers are estimates averaged over months and grouped into ranges, so treat them as relative, not exact. What matters more is the match between a keyword's intent and the page you create: Google tries to understand the meaning behind a query and groups similar phrasings together, which is why one well-built page can rank for dozens of related long-tail searches. Mapping one primary keyword per page prevents keyword cannibalisation, where two of your own pages split relevance signals and both rank worse.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Create a keyword map of at least 15 keywords for your business using autocomplete, People also ask and Keyword Planner (or a free tool). Group them into 4–5 pages, assign one primary keyword per page, and mark intent and approximate volume for each.

docs.title: 06 · On-Page SEO
docs.text: On-page SEO is optimising each individual page so search engines (and people) instantly understand what it's about and why it's the best answer. You'll apply it to the pages from your keyword map.

docs.title: 1. Title tag and meta description
docs.text:
1. The title tag is the blue clickable headline in search results. Put the primary keyword near the start and keep it around 50–60 characters: Office Catering in Pune | Hot, On-Time, GST Invoice – Chai Corner.
  2. Every page needs a unique title.
  3. The meta description (around 150–160 characters) doesn't directly affect ranking but influences clicks: Snacks and meals for 20–100 people, delivered hot across Baner, Aundh & Hinjewadi. Per-head pricing from ₹120. Get a quote in 30 minutes.
  4. In WordPress, set these with an SEO plugin such as Yoast or Rank Math; in Wix/Shopify, use the page's SEO settings.

docs.title: 2. Headings and content
docs.text:
1. One H1 per page containing the primary keyword (often the visible page headline).
  2. Use H2/H3 subheadings for sections, naturally including secondary keywords and questions ("What's included in office catering?").
  3. Answer the search intent fully and early — price, area, minimum order — then add depth.
  4. Write for people: short paragraphs, bullet points, real details (menu items, photos, numbers). Don't repeat the keyword unnaturally; Google understands synonyms.
  5. Show experience and trust (Google's E-E-A-T idea: experience, expertise, authoritativeness, trust): real photos, named testimonials, address and contact details, author names on articles.

docs.title: 3. URLs, links and images
docs.text:
1. Short, readable URLs: /office-catering-pune, not /page?id=123.
  2. Internal links: link from related pages using descriptive anchor text ("see our office catering menu"). This helps Google discover pages and understand topics.
  3. Link out to authoritative sources when useful.
  4. Images: descriptive file names (office-snack-box.jpg), alt text describing the image ("Snack box with samosa, sandwich and chai for office meetings"), compressed and sized correctly.

docs.title: 4. Structured data and snippets
docs.text:
1. Schema markup (structured data) tells Google explicit facts: LocalBusiness (address, hours), Product, FAQPage, Review, Article.
  2. Many plugins add schema automatically; test pages with Google's Rich Results Test.
  3. A clear FAQ section helps you appear in "People also ask" style results.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Element Rule Title tag Primary keyword first, ~55 chars, unique Meta description ~155 chars, benefit + CTA H1 One per page, includes keyword H2/H3 Sections and questions URL Short, keyword, hyphens Internal links Descriptive anchor text Images File name + alt text + compressed Schema LocalBusiness, FAQ, Product; test in Rich Results Test

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Search engines read a page's structure the way a fast human reader skims: title and H1 for the main topic, headings for subtopics, links for relationships, structured data for unambiguous facts. Clear structure lowers the effort for Google to classify the page and for people to find their answer — and pages that satisfy searchers quickly tend to earn better engagement and links over time. Keyword stuffing fails because modern ranking systems model meaning; they reward covering the topic thoroughly in natural language.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Take the most important page from your keyword map. Write its title tag, meta description, H1, at least four H2s, a 400-word draft body with real details, three internal links, alt text for two images, and a five-question FAQ. If the page is live, re-check it in URL inspection after publishing.

docs.title: 07 · Social Media Marketing Basics
docs.text: Social media is where people discover brands, build trust and talk back. This module shows you how to choose platforms, plan content that people actually engage with, and measure it — without burning out.

docs.title: 1. Choose platforms by audience
docs.text:
1. Instagram — visual, Reels-driven; strong for food, fashion, lifestyle, local businesses and creators.
  2. Facebook — older audiences, local groups, events; still powerful for ads.
  3. YouTube — search-driven video, tutorials, long-form trust (Level 2, Module 6).
  4. LinkedIn — B2B, professionals, hiring; ideal for Chai Corner's office catering persona.
  5. WhatsApp Business — catalogue, quick replies, broadcast lists, Status; essential in India for conversations.
  6. Start with two platforms where your persona already spends time. Doing two well beats five badly.

docs.title: 2. Set up profiles properly
docs.text:
1. Consistent name, logo and handle across platforms.
  2. Bio: what you offer, for whom, location, and a CTA with a link (website or WhatsApp).
  3. Switch Instagram to a Professional (Business) account for insights and contact buttons.
  4. Fill in hours, address, categories and highlight stories (Menu, Reviews, Catering, How to order).

docs.title: 3. Plan content with pillars
docs.text:
1. Pick 3–5 content pillars tied to your persona: Behind the scenes (making samosas at 7 am), Proof (office orders delivered, reviews), Value (snack ideas for meetings), Offers (weekday combo), Community (regular customers, local events).
  2. Mix formats: Reels/short video (highest reach), carousels (saves and shares), single images, Stories (daily touchpoints, polls), Lives.
  3. Use a simple monthly content calendar: date, pillar, format, caption idea, CTA, status.
  4. A realistic rhythm for a small business: 3–4 posts a week plus daily Stories.
  5. Hooks matter: the first 1–2 seconds of a Reel and the first line of a caption decide whether people stop scrolling.

docs.title: 4. Engage and measure
docs.text:
1. Reply to comments and DMs quickly — engagement in the first hour helps reach.
  2. Use relevant hashtags (a handful, specific: #PuneFood #BanerCafe) and location tags.
  3. Collaborate: Instagram Collab posts with local creators or partner businesses.
  4. Measure weekly in Insights: reach, engagement rate (interactions ÷ reach), saves, shares, profile visits, link clicks, and messages that turn into orders.
  5. Double down on formats and topics that earn saves and shares; drop what doesn't perform after a fair test (4–6 posts).

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Item Guideline Platforms Start with 2 where your persona is Bio Offer + audience + location + CTA link Pillars 3–5 recurring themes Formats Reels for reach, carousels for saves, Stories daily Engagement rate Interactions ÷ reach Cadence 3–4 posts/week + Stories Review Weekly insights; keep what's saved/shared

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Social feeds are ranked by recommendation systems that predict how likely each person is to watch, like, comment, share or save a post. Early signals — watch time in the first seconds, shares to friends, saves — tell the system the content is worth showing to more people, including non-followers. That's why hooks and genuinely useful or entertaining content outperform polished ads: the algorithm distributes what people engage with, not what brands want to say.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Set up (or audit) two social profiles for your business. Define four content pillars and create a two-week calendar with at least 8 posts and daily Story ideas, including two Reels scripts with a hook for the first two seconds. After posting (if possible), record reach and engagement rate for each post.

docs.title: 08 · Email Marketing Basics
docs.text: Email is the channel you own: no algorithm decides whether your subscribers see your message. Done well, it's the cheapest way to turn interested people into customers and customers into regulars. This module covers building a list, writing emails people open, and measuring results.

docs.title: 1. Build a permission-based list
docs.text:
1. Only email people who opted in. Buying lists hurts deliverability and breaks laws such as India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and anti-spam rules in other countries.
  2. Offer a reason to subscribe (a lead magnet): "Office snack menu + price list PDF", "10% off your first catering order", a monthly recipe.
  3. Add sign-up forms to the website, landing page and thank-you page; collect only name and email (and consent).
  4. Use an email platform: Mailchimp, Brevo, MailerLite, Zoho Campaigns or ConvertKit — all have free tiers.

docs.title: 2. Write emails that get opened and clicked
docs.text:
1. Sender name people recognise: "Neha at Chai Corner" often beats "info".
  2. Subject line (30–50 characters): specific and useful — "This Friday's office snack menu (from ₹120)".
  3. Preview text: the line shown after the subject; use it to add a second reason to open.
  4. One main message and one CTA per email: "Book Friday's order".
  5. Short paragraphs, a clear button, mobile-friendly layout (most emails are read on phones).
  6. Always include your address and an easy unsubscribe link.

docs.title: 3. Types of email
docs.text:
1. Welcome email — sent immediately after sign-up; deliver the lead magnet, set expectations, highest open rates you'll get.
  2. Newsletter — regular value plus a light offer.
  3. Promotional — a time-bound offer or launch.
  4. Transactional — order confirmations, invoices; reliable and expected.
  5. Re-engagement — "Still want our menus?" to inactive subscribers; remove those who never open to protect deliverability.

docs.title: 4. Measure and improve
docs.text:
1. Open rate — opens ÷ delivered. Apple's Mail Privacy Protection inflates opens, so treat it as a rough signal.
  2. Click-through rate (CTR) — clicks ÷ delivered; a more reliable engagement metric.
  3. Conversion rate — orders or bookings from the email (track with UTM links — Level 2, Module 8).
  4. Unsubscribe and spam complaint rates — keep complaints well under 0.1%.
  5. A/B test one variable at a time, such as two subject lines on a sample before sending the winner to everyone.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Item Guideline Permission Opt-in only; consent recorded Lead magnet Useful freebie or discount Subject 30–50 chars, specific Preview text Second reason to open Body One message, one CTA, mobile-first Footer Address + unsubscribe Metrics CTR, conversions, unsubscribes, complaints

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Inbox providers like Gmail decide whether your email lands in the primary tab, promotions or spam based on sender reputation: authentication records on your domain (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), how many recipients open and engage, and how many delete without reading or mark you as spam. Sending relevant emails to people who asked for them builds reputation; blasting cold or inactive addresses destroys it. Gmail and Yahoo now require bulk senders to authenticate their domain and provide one-click unsubscribe, so setting up your platform's domain authentication is part of email marketing, not an optional extra.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Create a free account on an email platform, set up a sign-up form with a lead magnet idea, and write a welcome email (subject, preview text, body, CTA) plus one newsletter for your persona. Send test emails to yourself on desktop and mobile and fix anything that looks broken.

docs.title: 09 · Google Analytics 4 Basics
docs.text: Google Analytics 4 (GA4) shows who visits your website, where they came from and what they do. Without measurement, you can't tell which channel or campaign is working. This module sets up GA4 and teaches the reports you'll use weekly.

docs.title: 1. Create a property and install the tag
docs.text:
1. Go to analytics.google.com, create an account, then a GA4 property (set your country and currency, e.g. India, INR).
  2. Create a Web data stream for your website URL. GA4 gives you a Measurement ID (G-XXXXXXX).
  3. Install the tag: in WordPress use the Site Kit by Google plugin; in Wix/Shopify paste the Measurement ID in the analytics settings; or add the Google tag snippet to every page's <head>. Google Tag Manager is the flexible option for later.
  4. Keep Enhanced measurement on — it automatically tracks page views, scrolls, outbound clicks, site search, video engagement and file downloads.
  5. Open Reports → Realtime and visit your site from your phone; you should appear within a minute.

docs.title: 2. The reports you'll use
docs.text:
1. Reports → Acquisition → Traffic acquisition — sessions by channel: Organic Search, Direct, Paid Search, Organic Social, Referral, Email.
  2. Reports → Engagement → Pages and screens — which pages get views and how long people engage.
  3. Reports → User attributes / Tech — country, city, device (mobile vs desktop).
  4. Engagement rate — share of sessions that lasted over 10 seconds, viewed 2+ pages, or triggered a conversion. It replaced "bounce rate" as the main quality signal (bounce rate = the opposite).
  5. Set the date range (top right) and compare to the previous period to spot trends.

docs.title: 3. Key events (conversions)
docs.text:
1. GA4 is event-based: every interaction is an event.
  2. Mark the actions that matter as key events (Admin → Events → mark as key event), e.g. generate_lead when the catering form is submitted or the thank-you page loads.
  3. A simple no-code method: create an event that fires when the page path contains /thank-you (Admin → Events → Create event), then mark it as a key event.
  4. Now Traffic acquisition shows key events per channel — which sources bring enquiries, not just visits.

docs.title: 4. Privacy and good hygiene
docs.text:
1. Add a privacy policy explaining analytics and cookies.
  2. Exclude your own visits where possible (Admin → Data streams → Configure tag settings → Define internal traffic) so they don't skew data.
  3. Link GA4 with Search Console and later Google Ads (Admin → Product links) to see search queries and ad performance in one place.
  4. Data retention: set event data retention to the maximum available (Admin → Data retention) so explorations can look further back.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Task Where Measurement ID Admin → Data streams Live check Reports → Realtime Channels Acquisition → Traffic acquisition Top pages Engagement → Pages and screens Mark conversions Admin → Events → key event Link Search Console / Ads Admin → Product links Exclude own traffic Data stream → tag settings → internal traffic

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: When a page loads, the Google tag sends small event messages (page_view, scroll, click) with an anonymous identifier stored in a first-party cookie, plus information like the referring site and campaign parameters. GA4 groups these events into sessions and users, then assigns each session to a channel using rules about the source and medium (for example, a visit from google.com without ad parameters is Organic Search). Because cookies can be blocked or cleared and some users decline consent, analytics is a strong directional signal rather than a perfect count — compare trends and ratios, not single numbers.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Install GA4 on a site you control, confirm your visit in Realtime, and create a key event for a thank-you page or form submission. After a week, write down sessions by channel, the top five pages, mobile vs desktop share, and engagement rate.

docs.title: 10 · Project — Launch Plan for a Local Business
docs.text: Time to combine everything from Level 1 into one deliverable: a 90-day digital marketing launch plan for a real local business. This is the kind of document freelancers and junior marketers present to clients, so make it good enough to show.

docs.title: 1. Choose the business and goal
docs.text:
1. Pick a real local business (a café, coaching centre, clinic, salon, boutique, repair shop). If possible, work with the owner.
  2. Write a SMART goal (Module 1): e.g. "Get 40 new trial-class enquiries per month for a dance academy in Kochi within 90 days at under ₹250 per lead."
  3. Record the current baseline: monthly enquiries, website visits, followers, Google reviews.

docs.title: 2. Audience and message
docs.text:
1. One primary persona and one secondary (Module 2), each with goals, pains, channels, objections.
  2. A short journey map with the three biggest drop-off risks.
  3. The value proposition sentence and a headline.

docs.title: 3. Website and SEO plan
docs.text:
1. Audit the current site with the five-second checklist and PageSpeed (Module 3). List the top five fixes.
  2. Outline one landing page for the main offer: headline, benefits, proof, FAQ, CTA.
  3. A keyword map of 15+ keywords across 4–5 pages (Module 5).
  4. Title tags, meta descriptions and H1s for the three most important pages (Module 6).
  5. Confirm Search Console is set up and the sitemap submitted (Module 4).

docs.title: 4. Social and email plan
docs.text:
1. Two chosen social platforms and why (Module 7).
  2. Four content pillars and a four-week content calendar (12+ posts, Story ideas, two Reel scripts).
  3. A lead magnet, sign-up form placement and a welcome email plus two newsletters (Module 8).

docs.title: 5. Measurement
docs.text:
1. GA4 installed, with a key event for enquiries (Module 9).
  2. A weekly scorecard: sessions by channel, enquiries, conversion rate, social reach, email sign-ups.
  3. A 90-day timeline: Weeks 1–2 fixes and setup; Weeks 3–8 content and SEO; Weeks 9–12 review, double down on what works.

docs.title: Deliverable checklist
docs.text: Section Done? SMART goal + baseline Personas + journey + value proposition Website audit + landing page outline Keyword map + on-page for 3 pages Social pillars + 4-week calendar Lead magnet + 3 emails GA4 key event + weekly scorecard 90-day timeline

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A good launch plan is a chain of assumptions you can test: this persona searches these keywords, this page converts them at roughly this rate, this channel reaches them at this cost. Writing the chain down — with a baseline and a scorecard — is what turns marketing from guesswork into a system you can improve each week. Clients and employers value the plan less for its predictions than for showing that you know what to measure and how you'll adjust.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Produce the full plan as a document or slide deck (8–12 pages) using the checklist above. If you're working with a real owner, present it to them and record their feedback — then revisit your numbers after 30 days to see which assumptions held.

docs.title: Level 2 · Intermediate Core Channels
docs.text: Goal: run each major channel properly — search ads, social ads, content, local SEO and email automation — and measure every result.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Technical SEO
  2. Local SEO & Google Business Profile
  3. Content Marketing Strategy
  4. Google Ads: Search Campaigns
  5. Meta Ads (Facebook & Instagram)
  6. YouTube & Video Marketing
  7. Email Automation & Segmentation
  8. Conversion Tracking: GA4 Events & UTMs
  9. Conversion Rate Optimization Basics
  10. Project — A Small-Budget Lead Generation Campaign

By the end of this level you'll fix technical SEO issues, rank locally, plan content, launch and optimise Google and Meta ad campaigns, grow on YouTube, automate email, track conversions with UTMs and GA4 — and you'll have run (or fully planned) a small lead-generation campaign.

docs.title: 01 · Technical SEO
docs.text: Great content can't rank if search engines can't crawl, index and load it properly. Technical SEO is the plumbing: site speed, mobile experience, indexing rules, site structure and errors. This module gives you a repeatable technical audit.

docs.title: 1. Crawling and indexing controls
docs.text:
1. robots.txt (at yoursite.com/robots.txt) tells crawlers which paths not to crawl. Never block CSS/JS or important pages by mistake; a stray Disallow: / hides the whole site.
  2. Meta robots noindex keeps a page out of the index (use for thank-you pages, internal search results, admin pages). Note: a page blocked in robots.txt can't be read, so Google won't see its noindex tag.
  3. XML sitemap lists the pages you want indexed; submit it in Search Console and keep it free of redirected or noindexed URLs.
  4. Canonical tags (<link rel="canonical" href="...">) tell Google which URL is the main version when similar pages exist (e.g. product pages with sort/filter parameters).
  5. Check Search Console → Pages for reasons like "Crawled – currently not indexed", "Duplicate without user-selected canonical", or "Blocked by robots.txt".

docs.title: 2. Speed and Core Web Vitals
docs.text:
1. Google's Core Web Vitals measure real-user experience: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint — main content loads; good ≤ 2.5 s), INP (Interaction to Next Paint — responsiveness; good ≤ 200 ms) and CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift — visual stability; good ≤ 0.1).
  2. See field data in Search Console → Core Web Vitals and per page at pagespeed.web.dev.
  3. Common fixes: compress and resize images (WebP/AVIF), lazy-load below-the-fold images, reduce heavy plugins and third-party scripts, use caching and a CDN, set image width/height to stop layout shifts, choose fast hosting.

docs.title: 3. Site structure and URLs
docs.text:
1. Keep important pages within three clicks of the home page.
  2. Use logical folders: /services/office-catering/, /blog/office-snack-ideas/.
  3. Add breadcrumbs (with BreadcrumbList schema) on deeper pages.
  4. Use 301 redirects when you change a URL so links and rankings transfer; avoid redirect chains.
  5. Fix 404 errors for pages that have links pointing to them (redirect to the closest relevant page).
  6. Ensure the site uses HTTPS everywhere and one preferred version (with or without www).

docs.title: 4. A simple technical audit
docs.text:
1. Crawl the site with Screaming Frog SEO Spider (free up to 500 URLs) to list status codes, missing titles, duplicate titles, broken links and redirect chains.
  2. Check mobile rendering with Search Console's URL inspection (view the crawled page screenshot).
  3. Review Core Web Vitals and PageSpeed for the five most important templates (home, service, product, article, contact).
  4. Prioritise fixes by impact: indexing blockers first, then speed on key templates, then structure and minor errors.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Issue Tool Fix Not indexed Search Console → Pages Remove noindex/robots block, add internal links Duplicates Canonical tags Point variants to the main URL Slow LCP PageSpeed Insights Compress hero image, cache, CDN Layout shift PageSpeed (CLS) Set image dimensions, reserve ad space Broken links Screaming Frog 301 redirect or update links Changed URL Server/CMS 301 redirect, update sitemap

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Google allocates each site a crawl budget roughly proportional to its size, health and popularity, then renders pages in a headless browser to see content loaded by JavaScript. Errors, endless parameter URLs and slow servers waste that budget and delay discovery of new pages. Core Web Vitals come from the Chrome User Experience Report — real visits by Chrome users — so lab tests only predict them; improvements show up in Search Console after enough real traffic over the following weeks.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run a technical audit on a site you control (or a friend's small business site): crawl with Screaming Frog, check Search Console's Pages and Core Web Vitals reports, and test three page templates in PageSpeed Insights. Produce a prioritised list of 10 issues with the fix for each.

docs.title: 02 · Local SEO & Google Business Profile
docs.text: For businesses that serve a city or neighbourhood, the map pack — the three local results with a map — often gets more clicks than the website results below it. This module shows you how to win local searches like "café near me" or "CA in Andheri".

docs.title: 1. Set up Google Business Profile
docs.text:
1. Go to business.google.com, search for your business; claim it or create a new profile.
  2. Choose the most accurate primary category (e.g. "Café", "Caterer") and relevant secondary categories — categories are one of the strongest local ranking factors.
  3. Enter the exact name (no keyword stuffing), address (or service area if you visit customers), phone, website and hours, including holiday hours.
  4. Verify the profile (video, phone, email or postcard depending on what Google offers).
  5. Add products/services with prices, attributes (outdoor seating, wheelchair accessible), and a business description.

docs.title: 2. Photos, posts and Q&A
docs.text:
1. Upload real photos regularly: storefront (helps people find you), interior, products, team. Profiles with recent photos get more engagement.
  2. Publish Updates (posts) for offers, events and new menu items.
  3. Use the messages feature or link WhatsApp if available, and answer common questions in your description and website FAQ.

docs.title: 3. Reviews
docs.text:
1. Ask every happy customer for a review: share your review link (from the profile's "Ask for reviews") on bills, WhatsApp and QR cards at the counter.
  2. Reply to every review — thank positive ones by name; respond calmly and helpfully to negative ones, offering to fix the issue.
  3. Never buy reviews or offer rewards in exchange for positive reviews — it violates Google's policies and consumer protection rules and can get the profile suspended.
  4. Review count, rating and freshness all influence both rankings and clicks.

docs.title: 4. Citations and local pages
docs.text:
1. NAP consistency: your Name, Address, Phone should be identical across the website, Google, Justdial, Sulekha, IndiaMART, Zomato/Swiggy, Practo (clinics), Facebook and other directories.
  2. Put full NAP and an embedded Google map on the contact page, plus LocalBusiness schema.
  3. If you serve several areas, create genuinely useful area pages ("Office catering in Hinjewadi" with delivery times, clients in that area, photos) — not copied pages with only the area name changed.
  4. Earn local links: chambers of commerce, local news, event sponsorships, partner businesses.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Factor Action Relevance Accurate primary + secondary categories Distance Correct address / service area Prominence Reviews, links, citations, brand mentions Profile Hours, services, photos, posts kept current Reviews Ask everyone, reply to all, never buy NAP Identical everywhere

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Google's local results are ranked on three broad factors it describes publicly: relevance (how well a profile matches the search), distance (how far the business is from the searcher or the location in the query) and prominence (how well-known the business is, using reviews, links and mentions across the web). You can't change distance, so local SEO is about removing doubt on relevance (categories, services, content) and building prominence (reviews and citations) faster than nearby competitors.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Audit or create a Google Business Profile for a local business: fix categories, hours, services, description and photos, write two Updates, and create a review-request message and QR card. List 10 directories and check whether the business's NAP is identical on each.

docs.title: 03 · Content Marketing Strategy
docs.text: Content marketing means publishing genuinely useful material — articles, videos, guides, tools — that attracts your audience, earns trust and leads to sales. This module turns random posting into a strategy with goals, formats and a calendar.

docs.title: 1. Content that serves the funnel
docs.text:
1. Top of funnel (awareness) — answer broad questions: "15 snack ideas for office meetings", "How much does office catering cost in Pune?".
  2. Middle (consideration) — comparisons and proof: "Café catering vs aggregators: which is better for a 50-person team?", case studies, menus.
  3. Bottom (conversion) — pricing pages, FAQs, testimonials, "How to book".
  4. Every piece should link naturally to the next step: a guide links to the catering page; a case study ends with a quote CTA.

docs.title: 2. Find topics people want
docs.text:
1. Start from your keyword map and People also ask questions (Level 1, Module 5).
  2. Ask sales or customer-facing staff: "What questions do customers ask before buying?" Each question is a topic.
  3. Check Search Console for queries with impressions but low clicks — content you could improve or create.
  4. Study competitors' best content (high-ranking pages, most-shared posts) and make something more useful, more current or more specific.

docs.title: 3. Create content that's worth ranking
docs.text:
1. Lead with the answer, then add depth (examples, numbers, steps, pictures).
  2. Add first-hand experience: your own photos, data, prices, mistakes and results — things a generic article can't copy.
  3. Use clear structure (H2/H3, lists, tables), a short summary, and internal links.
  4. Repurpose: one detailed guide → a carousel, three Reels, an email and a LinkedIn post.
  5. Update important pieces at least yearly; refreshed content often recovers lost rankings.

docs.title: 4. Plan, publish, measure
docs.text:
1. Build an editorial calendar: topic, target keyword, funnel stage, format, owner, publish date, distribution channels.
  2. Consistency beats bursts: one excellent article a week, or two a month, sustained for six months.
  3. Distribute every piece: email list, social channels, WhatsApp groups, relevant communities.
  4. Measure per piece: organic clicks and positions (Search Console), engaged sessions and key events (GA4), backlinks earned, and leads it assisted.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Stage Content types Goal metric Awareness How-to guides, lists, short video Impressions, organic clicks Consideration Comparisons, case studies, webinars Engaged time, return visits Conversion Pricing, FAQs, demos, testimonials Leads, sales Retention Tips, newsletters, community Repeat purchases

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Google's helpful content guidance and ranking systems aim to reward content created primarily for people, demonstrating real experience and expertise, and to demote content produced mainly to attract search clicks. Practically, pages that fully satisfy a searcher — so they don't need to go back and click another result — earn better engagement, more links and more shares, which compound over time. Content is an asset: a strong guide can keep bringing traffic for years, unlike an ad that stops the moment you stop paying.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Create a three-month content plan for your business: 12 topics mapped to funnel stages and keywords, with format, distribution channels and the metric you'll judge each by. Write one full piece (800+ words or a scripted 5-minute video) with real first-hand detail.

docs.title: 04 · Google Ads: Search Campaigns
docs.text: Google Search ads put you at the top of results for chosen keywords — immediately — and you pay only when someone clicks. This module walks through building a well-structured search campaign that doesn't waste money.

docs.title: 1. Account and campaign setup
docs.text:
1. Create an account at ads.google.com. Choose Expert mode (switch from the Smart campaign flow) to get full control.
  2. Link GA4 and set up conversion tracking first (Module 8) — without conversions, Google can't optimise and you can't judge results.
  3. Create a campaign: goal Leads (or Sales), type Search.
  4. Networks: untick Display Network for search campaigns to keep budget on search results.
  5. Locations: target where customers are (e.g. Pune, or a radius around the café). Under location options choose "Presence: people in or regularly in your targeted locations".
  6. Budget: start with what you can afford to test for 2–4 weeks (e.g. ₹300–₹500 per day).

docs.title: 2. Keywords and match types
docs.text:
1. Build ad groups around tight themes: "Office catering", "Party snacks", "Café near me".
  2. Match types: broad (Google matches related searches — use only with conversion tracking and smart bidding), phrase ("office catering" — searches including the meaning of the phrase), exact ([office catering pune] — same meaning as the keyword).
  3. Start with phrase and exact for control; add broad later when conversions are flowing.
  4. Add negative keywords to block wasted clicks: -jobs -recipe -free -training -course.
  5. Review the Search terms report weekly and add irrelevant searches as negatives.

docs.title: 3. Ads and assets
docs.text:
1. Write Responsive Search Ads: up to 15 headlines (30 characters each) and 4 descriptions (90 characters). Include the keyword, benefit, proof and CTA: "Office Catering in Pune", "Delivered Hot & On Time", "GST Invoice · From ₹120/Head".
  2. Add assets (formerly extensions): sitelinks (Menu, Pricing, Reviews), callouts ("Same-day orders"), call, location, structured snippets, images.
  3. Send traffic to the matching landing page, not the home page.

docs.title: 4. Bidding, Quality Score and optimisation
docs.text:
1. New accounts: start with Maximise clicks with a max CPC cap, or Maximise conversions if tracking is ready. Move to Target CPA once you have roughly 15–30 conversions a month.
  2. Quality Score (1–10, per keyword) reflects expected CTR, ad relevance and landing page experience. Higher scores lower your cost per click.
  3. Weekly routine: check search terms (add negatives), pause poor keywords, test new headlines, adjust bids by device/location/time where data supports it.
  4. Judge by cost per lead and lead quality, not clicks.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Setting Recommendation Campaign type Search, Display Network off Location Presence in target area Match types Phrase/exact first; broad with smart bidding Negatives Add weekly from search terms Ads RSA: 10–15 headlines, 4 descriptions Assets Sitelinks, callouts, call, location Bidding Max clicks/conversions → Target CPA

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Every search triggers an instant auction among advertisers whose keywords match. Google ranks ads by Ad Rank, which combines your bid with quality (expected CTR, ad relevance, landing page experience) and the expected impact of assets. The actual price you pay is usually less than your maximum bid — roughly what's needed to keep your position — so a more relevant ad can outrank a competitor who bids more while paying less per click. Smart bidding adjusts bids per auction using signals like device, location, time and the searcher's context to predict conversion likelihood.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Plan (or build, without launching) a search campaign for your business: two ad groups with 10 keywords each in phrase/exact match, 15 negative keywords, one full responsive search ad per group, four sitelinks and four callouts, location and budget settings. Estimate clicks and cost using Keyword Planner's forecast.

docs.title: 05 · Meta Ads (Facebook & Instagram)
docs.text: Meta Ads reach people based on who they are and what they're interested in — before they ever search. That makes them ideal for awareness, demand generation and retargeting. This module covers campaign structure, targeting, creative and tracking.

docs.title: 1. Set up Business tools
docs.text:
1. Create a Meta Business portfolio at business.facebook.com; add your Facebook Page and Instagram account.
  2. Create an ad account with INR currency and your time zone (these can't be changed later).
  3. Install the Meta Pixel on your website (Events Manager → Connect data source → Web) via your CMS integration or Google Tag Manager, and set up the Conversions API where your platform supports it for more reliable tracking.
  4. Verify your domain and configure standard events: Lead, Purchase, ViewContent, AddToCart.

docs.title: 2. Campaign structure
docs.text:
1. Campaign — choose the objective: Awareness, Traffic, Engagement, Leads, App promotion or Sales. Pick the action you actually want; Meta optimises for it.
  2. Ad set — audience, placements, budget, schedule and optimisation event.
  3. Ad — the creative (image, video, carousel), primary text, headline and CTA button.
  4. For lead generation you can send people to your landing page or use an Instant Form (opens inside Facebook/Instagram, pre-filled — more leads, sometimes lower quality; add a qualifying question).

docs.title: 3. Audiences
docs.text:
1. Broad / Advantage+ audience — give location, age and let Meta find buyers; often performs best once the pixel has data.
  2. Detailed targeting — interests and behaviours ("Office administration", "Small business owners").
  3. Custom audiences — website visitors (pixel), customer lists (uploaded, hashed), Instagram/Facebook engagers, video viewers.
  4. Lookalike audiences — people similar to your best customers.
  5. Retargeting: show a testimonial or offer to people who visited the catering page but didn't enquire in the last 30 days.

docs.title: 4. Creative that performs
docs.text:
1. Creative is the biggest lever. Make vertical 9:16 video for Reels and Stories, plus 1:1 or 4:5 images for feeds.
  2. Hook in the first 2 seconds, show the product in use, add captions (most watch muted), end with a clear CTA.
  3. Test 3–5 creatives per ad set; let Meta's delivery favour winners. Refresh creative when frequency rises and results drop (creative fatigue).
  4. Primary text: problem → solution → proof → CTA, in plain language.
  5. Read results in Ads Manager: CPM, CTR (link), cost per result, frequency; judge final success by cost per lead/purchase and lead quality.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Level Controls Campaign Objective (Leads/Sales/Traffic…) Ad set Audience, placements, budget, optimisation event Ad Creative, text, headline, CTA Tracking Pixel + Conversions API, standard events Audiences Broad, interests, custom, lookalike, retargeting Creative 9:16 video, hook in 2s, captions

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Meta runs an auction for every ad impression and picks the ad with the highest total value, combining your bid, the estimated action rate (how likely this person is to take your optimisation event) and ad quality. Its delivery system learns from conversion signals sent by the pixel and Conversions API, which is why accurate event tracking — and enough conversions for an ad set to exit the learning phase (around 50 optimisation events per week) — strongly affects results. Broad targeting works because the model, not your interest selection, finds the people most likely to convert.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Plan a Leads campaign for your business: objective, one broad ad set and one retargeting ad set, budget, three ad creatives (write the scripts or describe images, primary text, headline, CTA) and an Instant Form with one qualifying question. If you have a site, install the Meta Pixel and confirm events in Events Manager's Test Events tool.

docs.title: 06 · YouTube & Video Marketing
docs.text: YouTube is the world's second-largest search engine and a huge platform in India. Video builds trust faster than text because people see the product, the place and the person. This module covers channel setup, YouTube SEO, Shorts and measuring what works.

docs.title: 1. Channel foundations
docs.text:
1. Create a brand channel (not tied to a personal name) in YouTube Studio; add banner, profile image, description with keywords, links and contact email.
  2. Create playlists for your main topics ("Office snack ideas", "Behind the kitchen", "Customer stories").
  3. Add a channel trailer for new visitors: who you are, what they'll get, how often you post.

docs.title: 2. Plan videos people search for
docs.text:
1. Use YouTube search autocomplete and the Research tab in YouTube Studio's analytics to find what your audience looks for.
  2. Formats that work for businesses: how-to tutorials, product demos, comparisons, FAQs answered on camera, behind-the-scenes, customer stories.
  3. Script the first 15 seconds tightly: state the payoff immediately ("Here are 5 snacks your whole team will love, under ₹150 a head").
  4. Good audio matters more than a fancy camera — use a clip-on mic and a quiet room. Phones are fine.

docs.title: 3. YouTube SEO
docs.text:
1. Title — include the main keyword naturally and make it compelling (around 60 characters).
  2. Thumbnail — a custom image with a clear face or product and 2–4 large words; it largely decides click-through rate.
  3. Description — first two lines summarise the video with keywords; add chapters (timestamps like 00:00 Intro), links and CTA.
  4. Add captions (auto-generated, then corrected) and choose the right category and language.
  5. End screens and cards point viewers to the next video or playlist, increasing session watch time.

docs.title: 4. Shorts and measurement
docs.text:
1. Shorts (vertical, up to 3 minutes) bring discovery to new audiences; repurpose highlights from long videos and Reels.
  2. In YouTube Studio analytics watch: impressions click-through rate, average view duration, audience retention graph (where people drop), traffic sources (Search, Suggested, Browse, Shorts feed), and subscribers gained.
  3. Improve the first 30 seconds where retention drops most; test new thumbnails on videos with low CTR.
  4. Add links to your landing page with UTM parameters (Module 8) to measure leads from YouTube in GA4.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Element Best practice Title Keyword + promise, ~60 chars Thumbnail Face/product + 2–4 big words First 15s State the payoff Description Summary, chapters, links Captions Always; correct auto captions Analytics CTR, avg view duration, retention Shorts Vertical discovery; repurpose highlights

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: YouTube's recommendation system aims to maximise viewer satisfaction over time, using signals like click-through rate, watch time, retention, likes, surveys and whether viewers keep watching YouTube afterwards. A high CTR with poor retention signals clickbait and stops being recommended; strong retention tells the system the video delivers. Search traffic is driven by relevance (titles, descriptions, captions), while Suggested and Browse traffic — usually the larger share — depend on how well your videos keep viewers watching.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Plan five YouTube videos for your business with title, thumbnail concept, first-15-second script and description with chapters. Record and publish one (a phone is fine), add captions, and after a week note impressions CTR, average view duration and where retention drops.

docs.title: 07 · Email Automation & Segmentation
docs.text: Sending the same email to everyone wastes attention. Automation sends the right message at the right moment, triggered by what people do; segmentation tailors content to who they are. Together they turn an email list into a steady source of sales.

docs.title: 1. Segment your list
docs.text:
1. Collect useful fields at sign-up or over time: interest (office catering vs personal orders), city, customer or prospect.
  2. Use tags for behaviour: downloaded the menu, booked a tasting, ordered twice, inactive 90 days.
  3. Common segments: new subscribers, prospects who haven't bought, first-time customers, repeat customers, high-value customers, inactive.
  4. Send segment-specific content: office admins get bulk-order offers; families get weekend combos.

docs.title: 2. Build core automations
docs.text:
1. Welcome series (3–5 emails over 1–2 weeks): deliver the lead magnet, tell your story, show proof, answer objections, make an offer.
  2. Lead nurture for enquiries that didn't book: case study, FAQ, a limited offer, a personal check-in.
  3. Post-purchase: thank you, how to get the most from the purchase, review request after 2–3 days, cross-sell.
  4. Abandoned cart / browse (e-commerce): reminder within an hour, then a nudge with reviews or an incentive.
  5. Win-back: for customers inactive 60–90 days — "We miss you" with a reason to return.
  6. Birthday / anniversary — simple and well-liked.

docs.title: 3. Build it in your email tool
docs.text:
1. In Mailchimp (Customer Journeys), Brevo (Automations), MailerLite (Automations) or Zoho Campaigns: choose a trigger (joins list, tag added, purchase, date).
  2. Add delays, emails and conditions (if clicked / if purchased → branch).
  3. Add a goal or exit condition so people stop receiving sales emails once they buy.
  4. Test the whole flow with your own email before switching it on.

docs.title: 4. WhatsApp alongside email
docs.text:
1. In India, combine email with WhatsApp Business: broadcast lists for opted-in customers, quick replies, catalogues.
  2. For automation at scale use the WhatsApp Business Platform (via providers like Interakt, AiSensy, WATI or Gupshup) with approved message templates and opt-in.
  3. Use WhatsApp for time-sensitive, conversational messages and email for richer content; don't spam either channel.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Automation Trigger Goal Welcome series Subscribes First purchase Lead nurture Enquiry, no booking Booking Post-purchase Order placed Review + repeat Abandoned cart Cart left Recover sale Win-back Inactive 60–90 days Return visit Segments Tags + fields Relevant content

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Automations perform better than one-off campaigns because they're triggered by intent: a person who just subscribed or just abandoned a cart is thinking about you right now, so relevance and timing are at their peak. Segmentation raises engagement, which in turn improves sender reputation and inbox placement for all your emails. Exit conditions matter more than they seem — continuing to pitch someone who has already bought lowers trust and raises unsubscribes.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Design (in your email tool, or on paper as a flowchart) a five-email welcome series and a three-email post-purchase flow for your business, with triggers, delays, conditions and exit goals. Write subject lines and CTAs for all eight emails and define three segments with how you'll identify each.

docs.title: 08 · Conversion Tracking: GA4 Events & UTMs
docs.text: If you can't tell which campaign produced a lead or sale, you can't decide where to spend. This module sets up UTM parameters for every link you share and GA4 key events for every important action, so each rupee and hour is accountable.

docs.title: 1. UTM parameters
docs.text:
1. UTMs are tags added to a URL that tell GA4 where a visit came from: https://chaicorner.in/office-catering?utm_source=instagram&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=diwali_catering
  2. utm_source — the platform (google, instagram, newsletter, whatsapp).
  3. utm_medium — the channel type (cpc, social, email, referral, qr).
  4. utm_campaign — the campaign name (diwali_catering, may_offer).
  5. Optional utm_content (which ad or link) and utm_term (keyword).
  6. Use Google's Campaign URL Builder and keep a shared spreadsheet of naming rules: lowercase, underscores, consistent names.
  7. Don't use UTMs on internal links within your own site — they overwrite the original source.
  8. Google Ads auto-tags with gclid when GA4 is linked, so you don't need manual UTMs there.

docs.title: 2. Key events in GA4
docs.text:
1. Decide what counts: form submit (generate_lead), WhatsApp click, phone click, purchase, sign-up.
  2. Thank-you page method: Admin → Events → Create event, condition event_name = page_view and page_location contains /thank-you, name it generate_lead, then mark it as a key event.
  3. Click events (WhatsApp/phone buttons) are easiest with Google Tag Manager: create a GA4 Event tag (whatsapp_click) triggered by clicks on links containing wa.me, publish, and mark as key event.
  4. E-commerce sites should send the recommended purchase event with value and currency (most platforms do this through their GA4 integration).
  5. Test with GA4 DebugView and Tag Manager Preview before relying on the data.

docs.title: 3. Send conversions to ad platforms
docs.text:
1. Google Ads: import GA4 key events (Goals → Conversions → Import) or use the Google Ads conversion tag; set the primary conversion so bidding optimises for it.
  2. Meta: track the same action with the Pixel/Conversions API Lead event.
  3. Assign realistic values (e.g. average catering order ₹6,000 × 30% close rate = ₹1,800 per lead) so platforms can optimise for value.

docs.title: 4. Read the results
docs.text:
1. GA4 Traffic acquisition with key events shows leads by channel; add Session campaign as a secondary dimension to compare campaigns.
  2. Advertising → Attribution reports show which channels contribute along the path.
  3. Reconcile with reality monthly: compare GA4 leads with leads actually received in your inbox/CRM. Small gaps are normal (consent, blockers); big gaps mean broken tracking.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Parameter Example utm_source instagram, newsletter, google utm_medium social, email, cpc, qr utm_campaign diwali_catering utm_content reel_v2, header_link Key event generate_lead, whatsapp_click, purchase Testing DebugView, Tag Manager Preview

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: When someone lands on your site, GA4 reads the referrer and URL parameters to assign the session's source, medium and campaign; UTMs simply override the guesswork with explicit labels. A key event fired during that session is credited to those values (and, in attribution reports, to earlier sessions too). Ad platforms use the same conversion signals to train their bidding models, which is why one accurate conversion definition — shared across GA4, Google Ads and Meta — is the foundation of every optimisation decision you'll make.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Create a UTM naming sheet and tagged links for one email, one Instagram bio link, one WhatsApp broadcast and one QR code. Set up a generate_lead key event (thank-you page or Tag Manager click), test it in DebugView, and document how you'll reconcile GA4 leads with real enquiries each month.

docs.title: 09 · Conversion Rate Optimization Basics
docs.text: Conversion rate optimisation (CRO) improves the share of visitors who take your desired action. Doubling a landing page's conversion rate halves your cost per lead from every channel at once — usually cheaper than doubling traffic.

docs.title: 1. Find where people drop off
docs.text:
1. In GA4, build a funnel exploration (Explore → Funnel exploration): landing page view → scroll 50% → CTA click → form submit → thank-you page.
  2. Watch real sessions with a free tool like Microsoft Clarity (heatmaps and session recordings): where do people click, how far do they scroll, where do they rage-click or hesitate?
  3. Run a quick 5-second test with three people: what does the page offer and what should you do next?
  4. Read customer messages and sales calls for repeated objections.

docs.title: 2. Form hypotheses
docs.text:
1. Use the format: Because we observed [data], we believe [change] will [improve metric] for [audience].
  2. Example: "Because 60% of mobile visitors never scroll past the hero and the CTA is below the fold, moving a WhatsApp button into the hero will increase enquiries on mobile."
  3. Prioritise with ICE: Impact, Confidence, Ease (score 1–10 each, multiply or average).

docs.title: 3. High-impact changes to test
docs.text:
1. Message match — the headline repeats the promise of the ad or search.
  2. Clarity — say the price or a "starting from" price; remove jargon.
  3. Trust — testimonials with names and photos, ratings, client logos, guarantees, GST/registration details.
  4. Friction — fewer form fields, WhatsApp/call alternatives, autofill, no forced sign-up.
  5. Urgency and scarcity — only when genuine (limited slots, real deadlines). Fake countdowns damage trust and can breach consumer protection guidelines on dark patterns.
  6. Speed and mobile layout — faster pages convert better.

docs.title: 4. Test and learn
docs.text:
1. With enough traffic, run an A/B test (Level 3, Module 5) using your CMS, landing page builder or a testing tool.
  2. With low traffic, make the change, compare similar periods carefully, and look for big effects; or test on high-traffic ads first (headline variants) and bring winners to the page.
  3. Log every test: hypothesis, change, dates, result, decision. Learning compounds.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Step Tool / method Find drop-offs GA4 funnel exploration See behaviour Microsoft Clarity heatmaps, recordings Hypothesis Observed → change → metric → audience Prioritise ICE scoring Common wins Message match, price clarity, trust, fewer fields Record Test log

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Every conversion is a decision weighed between motivation (how much the visitor wants the outcome), ability (how easy the action is) and a prompt (a clear moment to act). CRO changes rarely create motivation — the right traffic brings that — but they remove friction and uncertainty that stop motivated people. That's why the biggest gains usually come from clarifying the offer and reducing effort, not from colour changes on buttons.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Install Microsoft Clarity on a site you control (or analyse a public landing page). Write five hypotheses using the template, score them with ICE, and implement the top one. If you can't measure a test yet, write the A/B test plan: metric, variant, duration and decision rule.

docs.title: 10 · Project — A Small-Budget Lead Generation Campaign
docs.text: This project combines Level 2 into one end-to-end campaign: tracking, a landing page, Google Search and Meta ads, nurture email and reporting. Run it with a small real budget (₹3,000–₹5,000 over 2–3 weeks) or build everything up to the publish button.

docs.title: 1. Brief
docs.text:
1. Choose an offer with a clear lead action: free trial class, catering quote, free consultation, tasting.
  2. Set targets: e.g. 25 leads at ≤ ₹200 CPL within 21 days, and at least 30% of leads qualified.
  3. Define what a qualified lead is (budget, location, timing).

docs.title: 2. Tracking first
docs.text:
1. GA4 with a generate_lead key event (Module 8), tested in DebugView.
  2. UTM naming sheet for all non-Google links.
  3. Google Ads conversion imported from GA4; Meta Pixel Lead event verified.
  4. A simple lead sheet or CRM: date, name, source, qualified (Y/N), outcome.

docs.title: 3. Landing page and nurture
docs.text:
1. A focused landing page (Level 1, Module 3) with message match for both ad sets, proof, FAQ and a 3–4 field form plus WhatsApp.
  2. Microsoft Clarity installed to watch behaviour (Module 9).
  3. A three-email nurture automation for leads who don't book within 48 hours (Module 7).

docs.title: 4. Campaigns
docs.text:
1. Google Search (Module 4): one campaign, two tight ad groups, phrase/exact keywords, 15+ negatives, RSAs with assets, location targeting, ~60% of budget.
  2. Meta Leads (Module 5): one broad ad set and one retargeting ad set, three creatives including a vertical video, ~40% of budget.
  3. Optional: boost organic reach with a Google Business Profile Update and a YouTube Short (Modules 2, 6).

docs.title: 5. Optimise and report
docs.text:
1. Days 1–3: check tracking, search terms, delivery; add negatives.
  2. Weekly: pause weak keywords/creatives, shift budget toward the lowest cost per qualified lead.
  3. Final report (2–3 pages): spend, leads, CPL, qualified rate, cost per qualified lead by channel, best keyword, best creative, landing page conversion rate, three learnings, next-month recommendation.

docs.title: Deliverable checklist
docs.text: Item Done? Brief with targets + qualified-lead definition GA4 key event + Ads/Meta conversions tested Landing page + Clarity Search campaign (ad groups, negatives, RSAs, assets) Meta campaign (broad + retargeting, 3 creatives) Nurture automation Lead sheet + final report

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Small budgets amplify noise: a handful of conversions can swing CPL wildly, and ad platforms' learning phases need data. That's why this project emphasises clean tracking, tight targeting, negatives and qualified-lead quality over volume — decisions are only as good as the signal behind them. The habit you're building is the core of performance marketing: launch, measure against a defined goal, reallocate budget toward what works, and document why.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run the campaign (or build it fully without publishing) and complete the deliverable checklist. Present the final report to the business owner or a peer, including what you'd do differently with double the budget.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Link Building & Digital PR
  2. Topic Clusters & Content at Scale
